title: Badge Clone — Network Infrastructure Room Access Confirmed

fields.to: All (Unified Command, Security, Operations, Public Information)
fields.summary: The forensic analysis of the cloned badge's access events confirms a targeted movement through secure areas. The clone entered Door S-4 at 07:38, traveled through Maintenance Corridor M-3, and accessed Electrical Room B (E-2) at 07:42. The individual remained inside E-2 for 12 minutes, from 07:42 to 07:54, before exiting via M-3 to Door S-6. The room is located in Concourse B and houses the fiber patch panel, primary network switch for Concourse B, and a wireless access point. No access to passenger zones, gates, or ramp areas was recorded. The movement pattern indicates deliberate targeting of network infrastructure, not random or opportunistic access. The attacker bypassed physical and digital access controls to reach a critical node in the airport’s internal network.

actions.text: IT confirmed duplicate badge event at Door S-4, 07:38
PACS log correlation completed; 125 kHz frequency identified as attack vector
Timeline of clone’s movement reconstructed from PACS and CCTV (SEC-NVR-01) logs
Electrical Room B (E-2) identified as target location; switch closet and patch panel confirmed as assets inside

planned: Immediate physical inspection of Electrical Room B (E-2) by Security and IT teams
Isolate VLAN 666 (Security Ops) from the rest of the network to prevent lateral movement
Initiate manual FIDS and BHS operations per TIRP Section 12.5
Activate FBI/CISA liaison per C2 guidance
issues: No physical evidence of forced entry in E-2; possible use of authorized access point (e.g., maintenance portal)
CCTV from M-3 corridor shows no individual in the video feed during E-2 access window; likely camera disabled or bypassed
Fiber patch panel not locked; staff may have left it unsecured

instructorNote: This inject confirms the convergence of physical and cyber threats. Watch for the IT team to request a joint inspection of E-2, and for Security to push for perimeter lockdown. The attacker used a known maintenance path — if the team doesn’t spot that, prompt them to cross-check the map.
